newsitem.title: USA: Brazil fiscal woes could hurt Argentine trade.
newsitem.headline: Brazil fiscal woes could hurt Argentine trade.

text.p: Fiscal problems in Brazil could easily disrupt the trade balance in Argentina, Richard Segal, director of emerging market fixed-income research at Santander Investments said in a recent report.
"Argentine exports have every reason to fear the consequences of policy slippage in Brazil," he said.

Brazil's Supreme Court last month ruled that 11 government workers were entitled a 28.9 percent wage increase granted to the military officers in 1993. If the ruling is applied to all civil service employees, Brazil's public sector's wage cost base would expand by tens of billions of reais, he said.
The Santander economist said the potential surge in wages could threaten the entire Real Plan, Brazil's anti-inflation program begun in July 1994.
"Should the Real Plan unravel, Argentina stands to lose big time," he said, adding, however, that this year would not be a concern.

In the period from 1993 to 1996, domestic demand in Brazil bolstered growth, while the net external trade balance deteriorated by an average of about 3.0 percent per year and current account deficits accumulated to about $40 billion, said Segal.
"During this time, Argentina's reliance on Brazilian demand resulted in a 10-percentage point increase in its share of exports destined for Brazil, from 22.9 percent to 32.5 percent," he said.
However, Segal asserted Brazil will not export inflation to Argentina, where the convertibility plan shields economy from inflation.
Additionally, a rise in Brazilian inflation could conceivably spur a rally in the Argentine local bond market, he said.
"Mechanically, this would occur through the drop in inflation and bank portfolio shifts from real to financial assets," added Segal.
But the benefit to Argentina would be limited if Brazil's inflation sparks regional economic uncertainty, causing capital flight from both countries, he said.
